overview: A linear actuator converts a motor's rotation into straight-line push/pull motion using an internal lead screw, so instead of a spinning shaft you get a rod that extends and retracts. The simplest versions wire up exactly like a DC motor — two wires, reverse polarity to reverse direction — while more expensive versions add built-in limit switches (to stop automatically at full extension/retraction) or a position-feedback potentiometer for precise intermediate stopping points. Key specs to match to the job are stroke length (how far it travels), force rating (how much it can push/pull), and speed (mm/s) — a common beginner mistake is picking one whose force rating is too low for the actual load once friction and gravity are accounted for.
simpleSummary: A motor that pushes and pulls a rod in a straight line, instead of just spinning.

specifications.speed: 5mm/s - 50mm/s depending on model (faster usually means less force)
specifications.feedback: None (basic), or built-in limit switches / potentiometer (advanced models)

pinMap.name: Motor+
pinMap.function: Motor power terminal; polarity determines extend vs retract direction.
pinMap.currentLimit: Model-dependent, often several amps under load
pinMap.gotcha: Needs a motor driver/relay rated for the actuator's stall current — actuators draw much more current when pushing against resistance or reaching the end of travel.

pinMap.name: Potentiometer Wiper
pinMap.function: On feedback-equipped models, an analog voltage proportional to rod position.
pinMap.gotcha: Only present on feedback-equipped variants — basic actuators have just the two motor wires.

useCases.title: Adjustable-height mechanism
useCases.scenario: Raise/lower a platform, camera mount, or robotic stand to a set position.

useCases.title: Automated hatch or door
useCases.scenario: Push a hatch or panel open/closed, using built-in limit switches to stop automatically at each end.

useCases.title: Precision positioning with feedback
useCases.scenario: Use the potentiometer feedback variant to stop at a specific intermediate extension, not just fully open/closed.

oftenConfusedWith: Solenoids (fast on/off push, not controllable position)
oftenUpgradedTo: Servo-driven linear stages (much higher precision, higher cost)
